direct_answer:
BASF states it conducted its first ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment in 2024, building on prior assessments but with greater granularity and documentation, and plans to update it annually [Source 1]. The process had three main steps: (1) compiling a list of potential sustainability matters relevant to BASF’s business/customer industries and stakeholder groups, with particular attention to higher-risk parts of the business/value chain; the assessment was performed at BASF Group level along the value chain and incorporated stakeholder interests via direct inputs (e.g., Advisory Councils, Civil Society Forum, multistakeholder networks) and indirect inputs (e.g., big data analyses of customer and capital market interests) [Source 1]. (2) identifying and validating risks and opportunities linked to impacts and dependencies with in-house experts and selected stakeholders (Nature Advisory Council and Human Rights Advisory Council), focusing on activities/sites/value-creation steps with elevated potential for negative impacts and risks; BASF also drew on its Group-wide opportunity and risk management and expert review of impacts/dependencies to identify additional risks/opportunities [Source 1]. (3) scoring impacts, risks and opportunities using predetermined criteria on a 5-point scale and classifying them as material when exceeding defined thresholds; impacts were assessed using a uniform framework covering severity, scale and scope, plus irremediability for negative impacts and likelihood for potential impacts, with a threshold based on the sum of factors and higher weighting for negative impacts; opportunities/risks were assessed for financial magnitude and likelihood, aligned with existing risk management methods; results were reviewed iteratively by interdisciplinary experts and risk-reporting experts, and governance bodies (Board of Executive Directors, Supervisory Board, Joint Works Council, Works Council Europe) were informed of process and outcome [Source 3]. After identifying material IROs, BASF mapped them to ESRS topic/subtopic/sub-subtopic (per ESRS 1 AR 16) and then assessed the ‘materiality of information’ at disclosure requirement/data point level using EFRAG criteria (‘decision-usefulness’ and ‘stakeholder relevance’) [Source 4].

Material sustainability matters identified as material from both an impact and a financial perspective are not explicitly listed in the provided passages. BASF does confirm that (i) climate change (E1) is material, with seven material impacts plus four material climate-related risks and two material climate-related opportunities identified [Source 5], and (ii) biodiversity and ecosystems (E4) was defined as material as part of the 2024 double materiality assessment [Source 8]. BASF also states that topics in the ‘Own Workforce’ category were defined as material [Source 11]. BASF notes that opportunities and risks identified have financial effects affecting financial position/performance/cash flow, and gives an example of financial effects arising in 2024 from a risk identified under ESRS S3 Affected Communities [Source 2]. However, the passages do not specify which sustainability matters are material in both dimensions (impact and financial) as a combined set [Source 2]. BASF also states ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users was assessed as not material [Source 2].
compliance_rationale: The retrieved passages provide a clear description of BASF’s double materiality assessment methodology, including value-chain scope, stakeholder inputs (direct/indirect), use of risk management, scoring criteria, thresholds, and governance review/information flows [Sources 1, 3, 4]. They also identify several topics as material (E1, E4, Own Workforce) and one as not material (S4) [Sources 2, 5, 8, 11]. However, the passages do not explicitly state which sustainability matters are material from both an impact and a financial perspective (i.e., the intersection of the two dimensions), so the second part of the question cannot be fully answered with the provided evidence [Source 2].
disclosure_gaps: Explicit list of sustainability matters that are material from both impact and financial materiality (the overlap/intersection), as opposed to being material in at least one dimension (not provided in the passages) [Source 2].
A consolidated results table (topic-level) showing, for each ESRS topic, whether it is impact material, financially material, or both (not included in the provided excerpts).

More detail on how affected stakeholders were engaged across topics; for biodiversity, BASF explicitly states affected communities were not involved in identifying material topics for that cluster [Source 8].
key_findings: BASF performed its first ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment in 2024, building on prior assessments with increased granularity and documentation, and intends annual updates [Source 1].
Assessment scope was BASF Group level along the value chain, with attention to higher-risk areas of business/value chains [Source 1].

Stakeholder interests were incorporated via direct engagement (Advisory Councils, Civil Society Forum, multistakeholder networks) and indirect inputs (big data analyses of customer and capital market interests) [Source 1].

Impacts, risks and opportunities were scored on a 5-point scale against predetermined criteria and deemed material when exceeding defined thresholds; impacts assessed by severity/scale/scope (plus irremediability for negative impacts and likelihood for potential impacts), and risks/opportunities assessed by financial magnitude and likelihood [Source 3].
Material IROs were mapped to ESRS topics/subtopics/sub-subtopics and then ‘materiality of information’ was assessed at disclosure requirement/data point level using EFRAG criteria [Source 4].

BASF identifies E1 Climate Change as material (seven material impacts, four risks, two opportunities) and E4 Biodiversity and Ecosystems as material; Own Workforce topics are also defined as material [Sources 5, 8, 11].
BASF states ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users is not material [Source 2].

BASF indicates financial effects arose in 2024 in connection with a risk under ESRS S3 Affected Communities, but does not provide a full mapping of which topics are financially material vs impact material vs both [Source 2].
